column2: # A reconcile-mode run may manage only what its OWN policy grants. That policy
# is excluded from the set reconcile can rewrite (it cannot widen its own
# grants), so the live policy drifts BEHIND the declared set the moment a new
# policy is declared -- and every read/write of the new name then 403s.
# Ask the server what this token can actually do rather than inferring it from
# the declared set, and fail LOUDLY naming the shortfall. Silently narrowing to
# what happens to work is the exact false green this block exists to prevent:
# a declared policy would never be written and nothing would say so.
# The prefix is added by matching '^' rather than capturing the whole name and
# substituting \1. A backreference does not survive the trip: YAML, Jinja and
# `command`'s shlex.split each get a say in what a backslash means, and the net
# effect was that all 60 paths rendered as the single literal
# `sys/policies/acl/1` -- a policy that does not exist, so the server answered
# `deny` and the gate concluded the identity could write nothing. It had never
# once asked about a real path.
- name: Ask the server which declared policies this identity may actually write
# sys/capabilities-self returns the per-path capability lists BOTH at the top
# level and under `data`, and which of the two a given client surfaces is not
# something to bet a hard failure on. Reading only `data` yielded an empty dict
# against a live policy that demonstrably grants create/read/update on every
# path asked about -- and an empty dict reads as ""denied everything"", so the
# gate blocked a converge that should have proceeded.
- name: Resolve what the server said this identity may write
# Keep only real policy paths, rather than removing a hand-listed set of
# envelope keys. The response also carries `capabilities`, `mount_type`,
# `mount_class` and friends, and any future field would join them -- a
# denylist would have to grow to stay correct. A stray key surviving here
# would be compared against declared policy NAMES below (the prefix is
# stripped, not filtered, at that point), so a collision would mark a policy
# writable that is not: a false green in the guard built to prevent one.
# An uninformative probe is NOT a denial. If the response carried capability
# entries for FEWER paths than were asked about, the probe itself is broken (a
# shape change, a malformed request) and reading the gap as a permission finding
# would be a confident false red -- the same absent-vs-denied confusion this
# whole block exists to eliminate. Fail, but say which failure it is.
# The count, not merely zero: the backreference bug asked about one literal path
# and got ONE well-formed entry back, so a `== 0` arm did not fire and the gate
# went on to report a unanimous false denial. A short answer is the direct
# signature of a probe that asked the wrong question, and neither a zero-check
# nor a type-check sees it -- the values were valid capability lists, just for a
- name: FAIL -- the capability probe did not answer about every path it asked about

writing only the reachable subset would leave the rest declared but never
written, with the converge still reporting success.
# Rendered on the CONTROLLER, not the target. The previous shape wrote each
# policy to the guest with `template`, read it back with `slurp`, and deleted it
# again -- three remote round trips per policy purely to move content this
# process already had in memory. Over 60 policies that is 180 operations on a
# proxmox_pct_remote connection, and each one is a full paramiko connect plus a
# `pct exec`: the render step alone measured 776 SECONDS (12.9 min, ~13s per
# policy) writing a few KB per file.
# `lookup('template', ...)` resolves against the same role templates/ directory
# the module used and renders with the same variable context, so the content is
# identical -- it just never leaves the controller. The write below feeds it to
# `bao policy write` on stdin, so no file is created and none has to be cleaned
# up. Remote operations for this phase: 180 -> 0.
- name: Render the RBAC policies on the controller
- name: Read existing RBAC policy contents
# Every other probe in this file tolerates a non-zero rc; this one did not, so
# a single denied read aborted the whole block before any policy was written.
# The map build below already guards on `rc == 0`, so a failed read is an
# expected, handled input -- not a reason to stop. The capability gate above
# is what turns a genuine scope shortfall into a loud failure.
# Both sides are `trim`ed and read from the CORRECT key, because the write below
# is a no-op only when the two compare equal -- and it was never equal:
#   * `bao policy read -format=json` returns {""policy"": ...} at TOP LEVEL. The
#     old expression read `.data.policy`, which does not exist, so every entry
#     resolved to '' and every policy looked changed on every converge.
#   * The server appends a trailing newline on write, so even with the right key
#     the stored text is the rendered text plus ""\n"" and an exact != is always
# Measured live: rendered 475 bytes vs stored 476, differing only in that
# newline, `stripped_equal` true on every sampled policy. Either defect alone
# rewrites all 56 policies on every run while honestly reporting ""changed"", so
# fixing only one would have looked like a fix and changed nothing.

column2: #                      readable by a fixed, low-privilege AppRole
# Non-secret configuration mount. Holds values that are sensitive-but-not-
# exploitable — operator selections, tunables, thresholds, coordination and
# inventory-ish facts — that today sit inside the credential mounts.
# It is a separate MOUNT, not a path prefix, for the same reason
# secrets-external is: a prefix shares one policy namespace, so every wildcard
# already granted on `secret/` reaches across it and the boundary is decorative.
# A distinct mount is unreachable by any policy that does not name it.
# Named `config` rather than a `secret*` sibling deliberately: an operator
# can tell at a glance which mount is not a credential store. A name like
# `secrets-internal-public` would blend into the credential mounts it must be
# KV v2 version retention for the config mount. Browsable history and rollback
# are half the reason this mount exists, so retention is set explicitly rather
# than left on the KV v2 default of 10. Config values are short strings that
# change rarely, so 30 versions is years of history at negligible Raft cost,
# while still bounding what a runaway writer can grow. delete_version_after is
# deliberately left at its default (0 = versions never time-expire): history
# that silently ages out is not history you can roll back to.
# Every KV v2 mount this role provisions (add-if-missing, then tuned to the
# declared retention). `max_versions` is optional — omit it to leave a mount on
# the KV v2 default, which is what the two credential mounts do today.
# External-SaaS credentials; a literal here for the same reason the policy
# Derived: the subset that declares retention. Defined once because init.yml
# zips it against its own read results — the two loops must be the same list in
# the same order, which two separate inline filters would not guarantee.
# Legacy demo subtree the terraform-proxmox vault-secrets proof writes to; kept
# writable by the terraform-apply policy so that read/write proof keeps working.
# App secrets PROMOTED into secret/apps/<app> so OpenBao is their canonical
# home. Each app maps each KV field to the converge-env var carrying its value.
# The promote step (init.yml → promote_app_secret.yml) runs only on the
# bootstrap host under the admin token, writes only when a value differs from
# what is already stored, and skips any field whose env var is empty — so a
# converge without those values (or with unchanged values) writes nothing.
# Promotion vs generation: a value that ALREADY EXISTS and must keep its current
# value goes here. A value that may simply be created fresh goes in
# openbao_generated_app_secrets below. Getting this backwards on a key that
# decrypts stored data destroys that data silently.

column2: # Random length for generated app credentials (alnum). secret_key needs more
# entropy than a login credential, so it gets its own length (matches the 64-char

column2: # Purpose: Configure log rotation for system and RKE2 logs
# which the distro's own rsyslog config already covers. logrotate refuses a
# duplicate log entry and aborts the whole run with ""found error in file rsyslog,
# skipping"", so the daily logrotate.service fails and nothing under
# /etc/logrotate.d gets rotated. They are driven by /etc/cron.d/logrotate-bloom
# with an explicit path, so a directory outside the include is enough.
- name: Create iSCSI aggressive logrotate config
# /var/log is root:syslog 775, which logrotate refuses to rotate into
# unless it is told whom to become. /etc/logrotate.conf carries the
# same ""su root adm"", but the cron job runs logrotate against this
# file alone and so never reads it: without this line every run ends
# in ""skipping ... because parent directory has insecure permissions""
# and syslog is never rotated at all.
# No dateext. A size condition rotates more than once a day on a
# busy node, and dateext names every archive after the day alone,
# so the second rotation of a day collides with the first and is
# skipped. The numbered suffix has no such limit and it is what
# the distribution uses for every other log here.
# No dateext, for the reason given on the iSCSI config above.
# The extensionless names are from the first version of this task, which was
# version switched to a .conf suffix without removing them, so int-test still
# carries both plus an .bak, and each one duplicates the same two log paths.
# One stale copy is enough to abort the whole logrotate run, so remove every
# name this task has ever written.
- name: Remove logrotate configs written by earlier bloom versions
# Neither job runs on minute 0, and no two of them share a minute. Both use
# logrotate's default state file /var/lib/logrotate/status, and logrotate
# takes an exclusive lock on it: a second logrotate that starts while the
# first still holds the lock exits with ""error: state file
# /var/lib/logrotate/status is already locked"". Three runs used to meet on
# minute 0, the two below plus the distribution logrotate.service, which
# logrotate.timer starts at 00:00. The error is collected in
# No -f on either command. -f forces the rotation whatever the config says,
# so ""size 200M"" and ""size 100M"" below never applied: every run rotated, and
# with the dateext the configs used to carry, only the first run of a day
# could, the rest ending in ""destination /var/log/syslog-<date> already
# exists, skipping rotation"". Without -f logrotate rotates when the file
# passes the size, which is what the two configs were written for.
# Offsets rather than a state file for each job: the iSCSI config and the
# distribution rsyslog config both name /var/log/syslog and /var/log/kern.log,
# and the one shared state file is what stops the size rotation here and the
# weekly rotation there from rotating the same file twice.
# iSCSI logrotate - runs every 10 minutes, on minutes 1 to 51
# logrotate for RKE2 logs - runs hourly, on minute 5
# imuxsock, a second load is rejected with ""module 'imuxsock' already in
# this config"", and the parameter was spelled SysSockRateLimit.Interval
# rather than SysSock.RateLimit.Interval, so it never applied either.
# No dynaFile=""default"" on the action: omfile takes file or dynaFile, not
# both, and no template named 'default' exists, so rsyslog disabled the
# action and the rate limit never took effect.

column2: # Installs and configures INetSim on the bare metal sandbox host.
# INetSim is a network simulation daemon that intercepts DNS, HTTP, HTTPS,
# SMTP, and FTP traffic from guest VMs and returns synthetic responses.
# It runs on the host, bound to the virbr-det bridge gateway IP, so guests
# can reach it but it is not reachable from the internet or management VPN.
#   1. Install the inetsim package (Ubuntu universe repo)
#   3. Deploy inetsim.conf (bind address, services, log paths)
#   4. Install a systemd drop-in that orders INetSim after libvirtd
#      (so the virbr-det bridge IP exists before INetSim tries to bind)
#   5. Enable and start the inetsim service
#   INetSim binds to {{ detonation_gateway }} (the virbr-det bridge IP).
#   This IP only exists after libvirtd starts and brings up the detonation
#   network. The systemd drop-in (step 4) enforces this ordering at boot.
#   During the Ansible run, the networking role runs before this role, so
#   the bridge is already up by the time this role executes.
# inetsim is in Ubuntu universe; ensure universe is enabled before running Ansible.
- name: Install dig (used to prove INetSim's DNS actually answers)
# INetSim 1.3.2 (May 2020, and upstream has not released since) calls the
# $pid is captured when the module is compiled — in INetSim's parent. INetSim
# forks a child per service, so the DNS child always fails that test, croaks,
# and exits 25. It had logged ""started"" one line earlier and never logs
# ""stopped""; its stderr is not wired to the journal. The result is a service
# that reports itself up and has never answered a single query, which is why
# loop_once is the other historical entry point: it does not call start_server,
# carries no pid guard, and creates its own sockets lazily. Verified on the host
# by replicating INetSim's structure (module loaded in parent, fork, child runs
# loop_once): the child survived, bound udp/5300, and answered a query with the
# This edits a distro-owned file, so it is written to be self-healing: `replace`
# re-applies after any apt upgrade that restores the original, and the assertion
# below fails the deploy if the anchor ever stops matching. Neither is the real
# guard — that is the live query at the end of this file, because a file that
# looks right is not a DNS server that answers.
# DNS.pm is ISO-8859, not UTF-8: one byte, 0xfc, the 'ü' in the German comment
# ""IP-Adressen für MX in Additional Section"". ansible.builtin.replace and
# lineinfile both decode the whole file as UTF-8 and abort:
#   'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xfc in position 7746: invalid start byte
# sed edits bytes, so it does not care. LC_ALL=C keeps it that way — under a
# UTF-8 locale, GNU tools can treat a file with an invalid sequence as binary
- name: Patch INetSim DNS to use loop_once instead of main_loop (#464)
# Only reached when unpatched, so the backup is always of a pristine file
# — including after an apt upgrade restores the original.
# '#' is the s/// delimiter here because ansible-lint's risky-shell-pipe
# heuristic reads a vertical bar anywhere in a shell task as a pipeline
# and demands pipefail — misleading to add to a task with no pipe in it.
# sed exits 0 when its pattern matches nothing. That silent no-op is the
# entire failure mode this task exists to avoid, so confirm the edit.
- name: Assert the DNS patch applied (a silent no-op here is the whole failure mode)
# Systemd drop-in — order INetSim after libvirtd
# INetSim binds to the virbr-det bridge gateway IP. That IP only exists
# after libvirtd starts and activates the detonation network. Without this
# ordering, INetSim starts at boot before the bridge is up and fails to bind,
# leaving guests with no network simulation until the service is manually restarted.
- name: Create systemd drop-in directory for inetsim
- name: Install inetsim systemd drop-in (require libvirtd)
# Ansible-managed: ensure virbr-det bridge IP exists before INetSim binds.
# libvirtd brings up the detonation network (and its gateway IP) at startup.
# The unit is generated from a SysV script whose `stop` kills only the PID in
# the pidfile and never removes it (init script line 81: `#rm -f $PIDFILE`).
# When the main process dies without cleanup the pidfile outlives it, the
# service children keep their ports, and every later start is a no-op that
# reports success. Observed here: the unit read `inactive` for 19 days while
# four children served traffic, and the #459 deploy could not restart over it.
# Full supervision fix is #463; this clears the specific state that makes a
- name: Clear a wedged INetSim (stale pidfile, orphaned service children)
- name: Enable and start inetsim service
- name: Flush handlers so the check below tests the restarted service
# The guard that matters. `systemctl is-active` was wrong in both directions on
# this host — `inactive` while four children served traffic, then `active` with
# no DNS at all — and a config file with the right port in it proves nothing.
# Ask the question the rest of the platform depends on: does a query get an
# answer? This is the check that would have caught #456 on day one.
- name: Verify INetSim DNS actually answers
# `dig +short` prints connection failures to stdout, so the grep is what makes
# an empty result mean ""nothing answered"" rather than ""answered with an error
# string"". failed_when: false because a non-answer must drive the retry below,
# not abort on the first attempt.
# .invalid is reserved (RFC 2606), so a real resolver could never answer this
# and a pass cannot come from anywhere but INetSim.",context/V007PILOT2-VARIABLE_REFERENCE_REASONING-021.md,,,,,,,,,,
